UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.		)		Docket No. ER26-2796-000
					)
Building for the Future Through	)
Electric Regional Transmission	)
Planning and Cost Allocation		)
COMMENTS OF AMERICANS FOR A CLEAN ENERGY GRID
(August 5, 2026)
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's ("FERC" or "Commission") Rules of Practice and Procedure, Americans for a Clean Energy Grid ("ACEG") respectfully submits these comments on Southwest Power Pool, Inc.'s ("SPP") Order No. 1920 compliance filing submitted on June 12, 2026. ACEG is a non-profit coalition representing utilities, hyperscalers, energy consumers, independent transmission and generation developers, and advocacy organizations united by a common purpose: expanding, integrating, and modernizing America's high-capacity transmission grid. ACEG applauds this filing by SPP as a significant step in developing more comprehensive regional transmission planning needed to address future challenges like the serious constraints and evolving demands on the grid that are currently raising prices throughout the region. When the Commission proposed Order No. 1920, it recognized mounting reliability challenges, capacity shortfalls, and accelerating load growth were straining an aging energy infrastructure. Today, those challenges have intensified. Robust long-term transmission planning is no longer merely desirable—it is essential. High-capacity interstate and interregional transmission infrastructure is fundamental to maintaining grid reliability amid unprecedented demand growth, ensuring efficient deployment of generation resources, and delivering affordable electricity to all customers.
Electric prices continue to rise throughout the country as demand grows rapidly after decades of flat load, due to generation retirements, an aging grid, and large load proliferation. Well-planned transmission is one of the most effective tools available to reduce costs for consumers. The grid must keep pace to maintain the nation’s competitive advantages, and planning decisions made now will lock in costs and reliability for decades to come. Modernizing and expanding the grid is essential to increasing reliability, being more resilient against extreme weather events, and keeping the lights on as systems begin to change. Additionally, delaying the build out of transmission is costly for both consumers and developers. For every $1B of well-planned transmission that’s delayed, consumers lose roughly $150-$370 million per year in net benefits that can’t be recovered. This cost of waiting to build out transmission will only continue to increase the prices of electricity for people across the country.
The recent Department of Energy (DOE) draft National Transmission Needs Study reinforces the premises underlying Order No. 1920 as well. DOE identifies load growth as the primary driver of future transmission need nationwide and concludes that “[l]ong-term regional and interregional transmission needs should be identified through planning processes” that support load growth and grid reliability. DOE encourages planning entities to consider “a wider set of transmission infrastructure benefits” in their processes, finding that “holistic, multi-value transmission planning” can enable solutions that meet multiple planning objectives and produce a “more efficiently planned, cost-effective transmission system.” The Needs Study also documents what the nation has actually built. Of the transmission circuit-miles energized between 2016 and 2024, approximately 31% were rated at 69 kV and 35% at 138 kV, while only 21% were rated at 345 kV and 4% at 500 kV or above. Incumbent transmission owners built 98% of those circuit-miles, and roughly 40% of the total was driven by reliability needs. In other words, the historical build has been concentrated in lower-voltage facilities responding to near-term obligations rather than in the high-capacity regional backbone that long-term, scenario-based planning is designed to identify. That record is precisely what Order No. 1920 was adopted to change. 
	The SPP region confronts transmission planning challenges that make effective Order No. 1920 implementation especially critical. SPP is experiencing explosive, large-load-driven demand growth against a capacity-constrained system. SPP’s current system peak is 56 GW, and SPP projects this could rise to 109 GW within ten years—a near-doubling—with annual energy consumption potentially increasing by as much as 136%. SPP states plainly that its transmission system is at capacity, forecasted load growth will only exacerbate the existing strain, and that simply adding new generation will not resolve the challenge. Additional analysis corroborates both the magnitude and the driver. Grid Strategies’ 2025 National Load Growth Report attributes roughly 90 GW of SPP’s forecast peak growth to data centers, within a national forecast of 166 GW by 2030. It’s clear that this is large-load-driven growth—hyperscaler and industrial—arriving faster than the network was built to accommodate.
Additionally, SPP carries the most acute congestion-and-curtailment profile of any ISO. Curtailment in SPP has risen sixfold from 2020 to 2024, and SPP was among four ISOs—with CAISO, ERCOT, and PJM—that set annual curtailment records in 2024. SPP frames the consumer cost of inaction in its own terms: deferred transmission investment leads to higher congestion costs, increased curtailment of low-cost generation, reduced resiliency during extreme events, and heightened reliability risk. SPP cites Winter Storm Uri, during which day-ahead prices exceeded $4,200/MWh against a 2020 calendar-year average of $17.69/MWh, as illustrative of the volatility transmission mitigates. Resource adequacy concerns also exist: NERC’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment flags SPP for falling reserve margins as demand outpaces resource additions and identifies interregional transfer capability additions as mitigation for SPP’s seasonal capacity and energy shortfall risk.
Finally, interconnection on both the load and generator sides has been hampered by limited transmission. SPP's pre-Consolidated Planning Process (CPP) interconnection process had become unworkable: regional transmission planning and generator interconnection ran as two siloed, parallel processes, producing suboptimal solutions, repeated restudies, and inefficient cost allocation. By October 2025, the queue swelled to 552 active projects representing over 130 GWs amid relentless year-over-year growth in requests, straining a network already at capacity. On the load side, SPP has acknowledged it has been unable to study many transmission customers' requests for load additions because they lacked supply to cover the 10-year forecast, and that requested load additions are far outpacing its ability to study such requests. 
SPP has made significant strides to improve and unify its interconnection and transmission planning processes through the Consolidated Planning Process and its HILL, HILLGA, and provisional load interconnection processes. SPP cleared the backlog of requests dating to 2018 in September 2025, expressly framing that milestone as the precondition for transitioning to the Consolidated Planning Process, whose Planned Interconnection Location framework, GRID-C upfront cost certainty, and single decision point are direct structural responses to the withdrawal-restudy spiral. We note that SPP’s Order 1920 compliance filing maps well to many elements of the CPP and SPP’s existing tariff, which already contain many forward-thinking and effective elements to address its challenges. We also commend SPP for working closely with its state regulators in the Regional State Committee to develop a cost allocation method that both parties agree with and which was filed as part of SPP’s compliance filing. We encourage SPP to continue innovating and working to harmonize all these processes.
ACEG supports strong Order No. 1920 implementation that addresses SPP's transmission challenges and delivers benefits to customers. While supportive of SPP's overall framework and collaborative process, we offer the following observations where strengthened implementation could enhance outcomes.
COMMENTS
The Full Seven Benefits Assessment Must Occur When Alternative Solutions Remain Under Active Consideration 

SPP requests a deviation from Order No. 1920’s requirements governing when the seven required benefit metrics must be applied. Under SPP’s proposal, portfolios of Long-Term Regional Transmission Facilities are developed, screened, grouped, and optimized principally on the basis of Adjusted Production Cost (“APC”) savings; the full suite of seven benefit metrics is then calculated on the single, final consolidated portfolio after selection is effectively complete. SPP explains that its full benefit-metric analysis takes two to four weeks to run on one portfolio, that the 2026 ITP evaluated more than 9,000 candidate projects, and that applying the full metric suite during project selection would be “closer to impossible.” SPP further contends that APC captures roughly 85% of total quantified benefits, and that measuring portfolio-level metrics at the project-grouping stage would multiply the workload sixfold and extend the planning cycle by one to two months for limited incremental insight.
Order No. 1920 requires that the evaluation process “estimate the costs and measure the benefits” of facilities identified or proposed for potential selection, and that this benefits assessment occur at a point in time when alternative solutions remain under active consideration. Order No. 1920-A reinforces the purpose of that timing: transmission providers must be transparent about their evaluation of alternatives using the seven benefit metrics “so that stakeholders can understand why particular solutions or portfolios of solutions were or were not selected.” The requirement exists so that the seven metrics discipline the selection. 
We recognize that the operational concerns SPP raises are genuine, and we appreciate SPP’s candor in describing them. Respectfully, however, the filing as submitted does not yet demonstrate that this approach is consistent with or superior to Order No. 1920’s requirements. First, APC-led selection is not benefit-neutral. In a region defined by record wind curtailment and the highest congestion costs of any ISO, selection driven by production-cost savings may tend to favor congestion-relief projects while under-weighting the benefits that Order No. 1920 specifically required planners to measure — most notably Benefit No. 2 (reduced loss of load probability) and Benefit No. 6 (mitigation of extreme weather events and unexpected system conditions, including increased interregional transfer capability). Resilience- and reliability-driven facilities, whose value emerges collectively across a portfolio, are precisely the projects the Final Rule was written to surface; under SPP’s sequencing they may not compete on equal footing at the stage where the portfolio is determined.
Second, Order No. 1920 does not require the full seven-metric suite to be computed for each of 9,000 individual candidate projects; it requires that benefits be measured while alternatives remain under active consideration. SPP’s own description of the CPP identifies such a point: the stage at which need-specific project groupings and candidate portfolios are compared and consolidated. Measuring a disciplined subset of the required benefits across a handful of candidate portfolios at that stage is a smaller undertaking than SPP’s project-by-project framing suggests. 
Encouragingly, SPP’s own most recent planning cycle suggests it is better positioned to meet this requirement than the filing indicates. In the 2025 ITP, SPP developed a first-of-its-kind resiliency model — built with a dedicated Resiliency Strike Team — that isolated high-stress periods, applied system stressors, and generated three new quantified need types: LMP impact, transferability, and load shed. Incorporating those resilience benefits materially changed the portfolio’s economics, raising the benefit-cost ratio from 5.70:1 to 7.83:1 in Future 1 and from 9.36:1 to 10.82:1 in Future 2. This shows that SPP can quantify non-APC value — including the extreme-weather and transfer-capability value at the heart of Benefit No. 6 — within a single planning cycle and without breaking its schedule. If resilience value is large enough to transform the business case for the final portfolio, it is large enough to change which portfolio should be selected — which is why Order No. 1920 requires it to be measured while alternatives remain under consideration.
We urge the Commission to work with SPP to ensure the framework captures the full spectrum of benefits that proactive long-term planning can deliver. Should the Commission determine that additional information would assist its review — whether through a deficiency letter or otherwise — we respectfully offer the following areas of inquiry. The Commission could ask SPP to identify the specific point(s) in the CPP timeline at which alternative portfolios or need-specific project groupings remain under active consideration, and explain how the seven benefit metrics, or a defined subset, can be measured at that point. Additionally, the Commission could ask that SPP quantify the incremental burden of applying the benefit metrics to the small number of candidate portfolios under comparison at the consolidation stage — as distinct from applying them to thousands of individual candidate projects. The Commission could ask SPP to explain how the 2025 ITP resiliency analysis — which quantified LMP impact, transferability, and load-shed value within the planning cycle — could be adapted as a screening-level application of Benefit Nos. 2 and 6 during portfolio comparison. Finally, the Commission could ask SPP to describe how, under the proposal as filed, a stakeholder could understand why an alternative portfolio was not selected if the seven metrics are not computed for any alternative.
The Public Policy Cost Allocation Method Should Be Clear and Time-Bound
SPP proposes a new methodology for allocating the costs of projects associated with a state’s Public Policy Requirements. Under this method, SPP performs scenario analyses comparing a portfolio that includes Public Policy Requirements against one that does not, identifies and quantifies the resulting difference in costs by state, and allocates those incremental costs to load in the state or states from which the Public Policy Requirements emanate. 
ACEG supports the substantive design of this approach, however our concern is with when and how the method operates. As described in the filing, the allocation of incremental costs is made “as approved by the RSC,” and “[a]ny such cost allocation must then be filed with the Commission for approval.” Read together, these conditions mean that no allocation follows from the tariff itself. Each allocation instead depends on a future discretionary vote of the Regional State Committee and a subsequent 205 filing. A method whose operative result cannot be known until a later vote and a later filing occur is not predetermined in the sense the Order contemplates, and neither a state nor a developer can ascertain at the time of selection how the costs of a policy-driven facility will be allocated.
Additionally, the filing does not identify what governs if the Regional State Committee declines to approve an allocation or does not act. If the Highway/Byway methodology applies by default in that circumstance, the tariff would benefit from saying so expressly; otherwise a policy-driven facility could be selected in the regional plan with no applicable allocation method. Second, the proposal does not specify when the scenario comparison occurs, when the Regional State Committee is expected to act, or when SPP would make the resulting filing. Order No. 1920 ties cost allocation to selection, and additional clarity on timing would help ensure that the method remains anchored to that point.
We respectfully ask that the Commission confirm that acceptance of SPP’s public policy cost allocation approach constitutes approval of the methodology only and does not pre-approve any specific cost allocation subsequently filed under it. Additionally, we ask that the Commission seek clarification around the methodology applicable to policy-driven facilities in the absence of Regional State Committee action, and specify the timing of the scenario comparison relative to portfolio selection. These refinements would preserve the state-driven character of the methodology that SPP and its stakeholders developed while giving it the predetermined, self-executing quality that Order No. 1920 requires.
CONCLUSION

The challenges confronting SPP— significant large-load-driven demand growth against a capacity-constrained system, an acute congestion-and-curtailment profile, notable resource adequacy concerns, and constrained load and generator interconnection outcomes—are not abstract planning concerns. They represent concrete barriers to the reliable, affordable electricity that consumers, businesses, and the nation's economic competitiveness require. Order No. 1920 provides the framework to address these challenges through proactive, scenario-based planning that anticipates rather than reacts to evolving grid needs. SPP’s compliance filing establishes important foundations for this transformation, and SPP has demonstrated—through the CPP, its large-load reforms, and its collaborative work with the Regional State Committee—that it approaches these responsibilities in good faith and, in many respects, ahead of its peers. ACEG’s comments identify specific refinements that would strengthen implementation and deliver the Order’s intended benefits.
ACEG urges the Commission to ensure that Order No. 1920 compliance across all regions, including SPP, fully realizes the Order's transformative potential. The nation stands at an inflection point: unprecedented load growth from large loads and electrification, aging infrastructure requiring strategic replacement, and reliability imperatives that demand regional and interregional solutions rather than piecemeal responses. Strong Order No. 1920 implementation will determine whether transmission planning continues operating reactively—perpetuating interconnection backlogs, escalating costs, and market distortions—or pivots to the anticipatory, portfolio-based approach that customers deserve and grid reliability demands. The Commission has the opportunity and the responsibility to ensure that SPP and other transmission providers build the high-capacity grid infrastructure necessary to meet this moment. ACEG respectfully requests the Commission accept these comments and direct the refinements necessary to achieve Order No. 1920's full promise.

Respectfully submitted,

/s/ James Ritchotte
